title: Centaurorum et Lapitharum pugna
titleEn: Cyllarus and the Fall of Caeneus — Metamorphoses XII.378–535
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Nestor's account of the battle between the Lapiths and the centaurs runs to its end: Peleus and Nestor cut through the centaur ranks, the centaur Cyllarus falls to a javelin nobody can trace and Hylonome throws herself on the weapon that killed him, and Latreus taunts Caeneus with having been born a girl. When no weapon will pierce Caeneus, the centaurs bury him under whole forests, and Mopsus sees a bird rise out of the pile.

advisory.lede: At XII.470–476 the centaur Latreus taunts Caeneus with having been born a girl, with the deed and the price by which he says the man's shape was bought, and with what Caeneus suffered — the rape these lines point back to without narrating it.
advisory.more: Latreus opens by addressing him with the woman's vocative, Caeni, and says he will always be a woman to him; he asks by what act the reward was won and at what price the false shape of a man was got; he tells him to look at what he was born and what he suffered, to take up the distaff and the wool-baskets, and to leave war to men. Later Monychus calls him a half-male enemy. The text is given here unaltered and both English layers keep the contempt at the level Latreus and Monychus put into it, the female name and the jeer about spinning included. The alternative to an advisory is never a gentler translation.

sentences.t:
Ante tamen leto dederat Phlegraeon et Hylen
eminus, Iphinoum conlato Marte Claninque;
sentences.l: Yet before that he had given to death Phlegraeus and Hyles from a distance, Iphinous and Clanis with battle joined at close quarters.
sentences.i: But before that he had killed Phlegraeus and Hyles at long range, and Iphinous and Clanis hand to hand.
sentences.n: leto dederat, “had given to death”, is the ordinary poetic idiom for killing. eminus “at long range” is set against conlato Marte, an ablative absolute literally “with Mars brought together”, Mars standing for the fighting itself. Phlegraeon, Hylen and Clanin all keep Greek accusative endings. The verb is third person singular and its subject is carried over from before these lines; Nestor does not name him here.

sentences.t:
additur his Dorylas, qui tempora tecta gerebat
pelle lupi saevique vicem praestantia teli
cornua vara boum multo rubefacta cruore.
sentences.l: To these is added Dorylas, who wore temples covered with a wolf's skin, and the splayed horns of oxen, serving the turn of a savage weapon, reddened with much gore.
sentences.i: Dorylas is added to them — he wore his temples covered with a wolf's hide, and oxen's splayed horns that did duty for a cruel weapon, red with all the blood on them.
sentences.n: gerebat governs two objects: tempora tecta pelle lupi “his temples covered with a wolf's skin”, and cornua vara boum “the splayed horns of oxen”. praestantia vicem saevi teli is the set idiom vicem praestare “to serve in place of”, here “supplying the turn of a savage weapon”. rubefacta ... cruore says the horns are already blood-red when Dorylas comes into these lines. additur is a historic present passive.

sentences.t:
Huic ego (nam vires animus dabat) “adspice,” dixi,
“quantum concedant nostro tua cornua ferro!”
sentences.l: To him I — for my spirit was giving me strength — said, “Look how far your horns yield to our iron!”
sentences.i: To him I said, since my spirit was lending me strength: “See how far your horns fall short of our steel!”
sentences.n: concedant is present subjunctive in an indirect question introduced by quantum “by how much”, and concedere with the dative means “to yield to, to be inferior to” — so the taunt is a straight comparison of weapons. nostro is the possessive plural used for the singular, the poetic “our” for “my”: Nestor means his own blade.

sentences.t:
et iaculum torsi; quod cum vitare nequiret,
opposuit dextram passurae vulnera fronti:
sentences.l: and I hurled the javelin; and since he could not avoid it, he set his right hand in front of the forehead that was going to suffer the wounds:
sentences.i: and I hurled my javelin; and since he could not dodge it, he put his right hand in front of the forehead about to take the wound:
sentences.n: quod is a connecting relative, “and it”, picking up iaculum and standing as object of vitare; cum ... nequiret is the circumstantial cum with the subjunctive. passurae is the future participle of the deponent patior, agreeing with fronti — “for the forehead about to suffer”, a participle that predicts the blow before it lands.

sentences.t:
adfixa est cum fronte manus. Fit clamor, at illum
haerentem Peleus et acerbo vulnere victum
(stabat enim propior) mediam ferit ense sub alvum.
sentences.l: the hand was fastened together with the forehead. A shout arises; but him, sticking there and beaten by the bitter wound, Peleus — for he was standing nearer — strikes with his sword beneath the middle of the belly.
sentences.i: the hand was pinned to the forehead. A shout goes up; and as he hung there, undone by the cruel wound, Peleus, who was standing closer, struck him with his sword under the middle of the belly.
sentences.n: cum fronte is “along with the forehead”: the javelin nails hand and head together. Fit and ferit are historic presents beside the perfect adfixa est — Ovid moves in and out of the present through the whole of this battle. mediam ... sub alvum has the adjective doing the work of an English noun-phrase, “under the middle of the belly”.

sentences.t:
Prosiluit terraque ferox sua viscera traxit
tractaque calcavit calcataque rupit et illis
crura quoque inpediit et inani concidit alvo.
sentences.l: He leapt forward and, wild, dragged his own entrails along the ground, and trod on the dragged ones, and burst the trodden ones, and with them entangled his legs as well, and fell with his belly empty.
sentences.i: He sprang forward and in his fury dragged his own guts along the ground, trampled what he dragged, burst what he trampled, tangled his legs in them as well, and went down with his belly emptied.
sentences.n: The chain tracta ... calcata is a deliberate figure: each participle picks up the verb before it (traxit, calcavit, rupit), so the same act is named twice, once as verb and once as the object of the next verb. illis is ablative, “with those”, i.e. the entrails; inani ... alvo is an ablative of description, “with his belly empty”. terra is ablative of place, “on the ground”.

sentences.t:
Nec te pugnantem tua, Cyllare, forma redemit,
si modo naturae formam concedimus illi:
sentences.l: Nor did your own beauty, Cyllarus, ransom you as you fought — if only we grant beauty to that nature:
sentences.i: Nor did your beauty save you, Cyllarus, as you fought — granting that a nature like that can be called beautiful:
sentences.n: Nestor turns aside from the narrative to address the dead centaur directly (te ... tua, Cyllare): an apostrophe, and the second person keeps him present. redemit is literally “bought back, ransomed” — beauty failing to buy off death. si modo “provided only that” with the indicative concedimus is a real concession: the speaker doubts that a half-horse shape can be granted forma at all.

sentences.t:
barba erat incipiens, barbae color aureus, aurea
ex umeris medios coma dependebat in armos.
sentences.l: his beard was beginning, the colour of the beard golden; golden hair hung from his shoulders down to the middle of his forequarters.
sentences.i: His beard was just coming in, and golden in colour; golden hair fell from his shoulders halfway down the horse's shoulders.
sentences.n: erat incipiens is a periphrasis for a beard only starting to grow, and it marks Cyllarus as young. umeri are the human shoulders, armi the shoulders of the horse-body — one sentence for the two halves of him. aurea, at the end of line 395, is not completed by its noun coma until the following line.

sentences.l: A pleasing vigour in his face; his neck and shoulders and hands and chest nearest to the praised statues of craftsmen, and wherever he is man;
sentences.i: There was a pleasing strength in his face; his neck, shoulders, hands and chest came nearest to the admired statues of sculptors — and so did every part of him that is man;
sentences.n: The list of body-parts has no verb of its own: they stand in the nominative with the verb “to be” understood. proxima “nearest” takes the dative laudatis ... signis, so the comparison is with sculpture, not with other men. et quacumque vir est, “and in whatever part he is man”, is the hinge of the description — the praise so far applies only to the human half.

sentences.t:
nec equi mendosa sub illo
deteriorque viro facies:
sentences.l: nor was the horse's form beneath him faulty and worse than the man:
sentences.i: nor was the horse-body under him flawed, or inferior to the man:
sentences.n: facies is the subject, with the two predicate adjectives mendosa “faulty” and deterior “worse”; viro is ablative of comparison after the comparative, “than the man”, meaning than his own human half. sub illo, “beneath him”, quietly treats the human part as the whole self.

sentences.t:
da colla caputque,
Castore dignus erit;
sentences.l: give him a neck and a head, he will be worthy of Castor;
sentences.i: give him a horse's neck and head, and he will be a mount worthy of Castor;
sentences.n: The imperative da with the future dignus erit makes an informal conditional — “give him ..., and he will be”. dignus takes the ablative Castore. Castor was the horseman of the twin brothers, so the compliment is that this body would carry the best of riders.

sentences.t:
sic tergum sessile, sic sunt
pectora celsa toris.
sentences.l: so sittable is his back, so high is his chest with muscle.
sentences.i: his back is so made for a rider, his chest stands so high with muscle.
sentences.n: sessile, “that can be sat on”, is a verbal adjective from sedeo, a word one would use of furniture, applied to the horse's back. toris is ablative: tori are the bulging muscles, and celsa is “raised high”. The doubled sic ... sic gives the two proofs of the claim just made.

sentences.t:
Totus pice nigrior atra;
candida cauda tamen, color est quoque cruribus albus.
sentences.l: Wholly blacker than black pitch; the tail however white, and the colour is white for his legs too.
sentences.i: He was all over blacker than black pitch; the tail, though, was white, and the legs were white as well.
sentences.n: pice ... atra is ablative of comparison after the comparative nigrior. cruribus is dative of the possessor, “the colour is white for his legs”, i.e. his legs too have a white colour. Here quoque is the adverb “also”, not quo-que “and by which”; the same letters serve both words, and only the cases around it decide which you have.

sentences.t:
Multae illum petiere sua de gente, sed una
abstulit Hylonome, qua nulla decentior inter
semiferos altis habitavit femina silvis.
sentences.l: Many of his own kind sought him, but one carried him off, Hylonome, than whom no more graceful female dwelt among the half-beasts in the high woods.
sentences.i: Many of his own kind courted him, but one alone won him — Hylonome, and no more graceful female lived among the half-beasts in the high forests.
sentences.n: petiere is the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere for -erunt (petierunt); you will meet it constantly in verse. Multae is feminine — the suitors are the female centaurs, and petere here is “to court, to make for”. qua is ablative of comparison after the comparative decentior.

sentences.t:
Haec et blanditiis et amando et amare fatendo
Cyllaron una tenet;
sentences.l: She, both by coaxings and by loving and by confessing that she loved, alone holds Cyllarus;
sentences.i: She alone kept Cyllarus, by her caresses, by loving him, and by admitting that she loved him;
sentences.n: Three parallel ablatives of means: the noun blanditiis, then two gerunds, amando “by loving” and fatendo “by confessing”, the second governing the infinitive amare. Cyllaron keeps its Greek accusative in -on. una here is the adjective, “she alone”, and not the adverb “together” it will be a few lines later.

sentences.t:
cultus quoque, quantus in illis
esse potest membris, ut sit coma pectine levis,
ut modo rore maris, modo se violave rosave
inplicet, interdum candentia lilia gestet,
sentences.l: her grooming too, as much as can exist in such limbs — so that her hair is sleek with the comb, that she twines herself now with rosemary, now with violets or with roses, at times carries gleaming lilies,
sentences.i: She had her grooming too, as much as such a body admits: her hair smoothed with the comb, twining herself now with rosemary, now with violets or roses, sometimes wearing white lilies,
sentences.n: cultus, “grooming, adornment”, is left without a verb (erat understood), and the string of ut-clauses with the subjunctive spells out what that grooming amounted to. ros maris, here the ablative rore maris, is rosemary — literally “dew of the sea”. modo ... modo is “now ... now”, and the -ve ... -ve of violave rosave is “either ... or”. Magnus prints cultus, nominative; some editions print cultu, an ablative of respect, “in grooming too”.

sentences.t:
bisque die lapsis Pagasaeae vertice silvae
fontibus ora lavet, bis flumine corpora tingat,
nec nisi quae deceant electarumque ferarum
aut umero aut lateri praetendat vellera laevo.
sentences.l: and twice in the day she washes her face at springs slipped down from the crest of the Pagasaean wood, twice dips her body in the river, and drapes over her left shoulder or side no fleeces except such as suit her, and those of chosen beasts.
sentences.i: twice a day she washed her face in the springs that run down from the ridge of the Pagasaean woods, twice bathed her body in the river, and would drape over her left shoulder or side only such skins as suited her, and only from picked animals.
sentences.n: lapsis ... fontibus is ablative, “at springs that have slipped down”, with vertice “from the crest”; Pagasae was a Thessalian port, so the wood is in the centaurs' own country. quae deceant is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive, “such as would suit her”, and nec nisi restricts what she will wear at all. laevo is dative and can attach to either umero or lateri — the left shoulder, or the left side.

sentences.t:
Par amor est illis: errant in montibus una,
antra simul subeunt; et tum Lapitheia tecta
intrarant pariter, pariter fera bella gerebant.
sentences.l: Equal is the love for them: they wander in the mountains together, they go into caves at the same time; and then they had entered the Lapith halls side by side, side by side they were waging the fierce war.
sentences.i: Their love was matched on both sides: they roamed the mountains together, went into the caves together; and that day they had entered the Lapith house side by side, and side by side were fighting the savage battle.
sentences.n: illis is dative of the person concerned, “the love is equal for them”, i.e. the same on both sides. una, simul, pariter and pariter again are four words for “together” in three lines: the point is made by repetition. intrarant is syncopated for intraverant. The pluperfect and the imperfect gerebant set the finished entry against the fighting still going on.

sentences.l: The author is in uncertainty: a javelin came from the left side and, lower down, where the chest lies beneath the neck, it pierced you, Cyllarus;
sentences.i: Who threw it is unknown: a javelin came from the left and struck you, Cyllarus, low down, where the chest runs under the neck;
sentences.n: Auctor in incerto est is an idiom — “the doer is in uncertainty”, i.e. nobody could say who threw it. inferius is the comparative adverb “lower down”; qua is the relative adverb “where”, and collo is dative after subsunt “lie beneath”. The apostrophe returns at the moment of the wound: Nestor addresses Cyllarus again. Magnus prints qua “where”; some editions print quam, which would make it “lower than”, comparative with inferius.

sentences.t:
parvo cor vulnere laesum
corpore cum toto post tela educta refrixit.
sentences.l: the heart, injured by a small wound, together with the whole body grew cold after the weapon was drawn out.
sentences.i: the heart, hurt by that small wound, went cold along with the whole body once the weapon had been pulled out.
sentences.n: cor is the subject and laesum agrees with it. corpore cum toto puts the preposition second, an ordinary poetic inversion. post tela educta is the participial phrase Latin prefers to an abstract noun — “after the weapons drawn out” = “after the drawing out of the weapon”. refrixit is the perfect of refrigesco, “grew cold again”.

sentences.t:
Protinus Hylonome morientes excipit artus
inpositaque manu vulnus fovet oraque ad ora
admovet atque animae fugienti obsistere temptat.
sentences.l: At once Hylonome catches the dying limbs and, her hand laid on, warms the wound and brings mouth to mouth and tries to stand in the way of the fleeing breath.
sentences.i: At once Hylonome caught his dying body, laid her hand on the wound and warmed it, brought her mouth to his, and tried to block the escaping breath.
sentences.n: Four historic presents — excipit, fovet, admovet, temptat — put the scene in front of us. inposita ... manu is an ablative absolute, “her hand having been laid on”. fovet is “keeps warm, cherishes”, set against the refrixit “grew cold” of the sentence before. obsistere takes the dative animae fugienti, and anima is both the breath and the life.

sentences.t:
Ut videt exstinctum, dictis, quae clamor ad aures
arcuit ire meas, telo, quod inhaeserat illi,
incubuit moriensque suum conplexa maritum est.
sentences.l: When she sees him extinguished, with words which the shouting kept from coming to my ears, she fell upon the weapon which had stuck fast in him, and dying embraced her own husband.
sentences.i: When she saw that he was dead, she said something the uproar kept from reaching my ears, and threw herself on the weapon still fixed in him, and died embracing her husband.
sentences.n: Ut with the indicative videt is temporal, “when”. dictis is an ablative of attendant circumstance, “with words”, and quae is their object with arcuit ire, “kept them from going” — arceo with a bare infinitive is poetic. incubuit takes the dative telo, “fell upon the weapon”. conplexa is the perfect participle of the deponent conplector and is active in sense, “having embraced”, of her; conp- is the edition's own spelling.

sentences.t:
Ante oculos stat et ille meos, qui sena leonum
vinxerat inter se conexis vellera nodis,
Phaeocomes, hominemque simul protectus equumque.
sentences.l: Before my eyes stands that one too who had bound six lions' fleeces with knots joined to one another, Phaeocomes, protected as to man and horse at once.
sentences.i: That one too stands before my eyes: Phaeocomes, who had fastened six lion-skins together with interlocking knots, and so was covered, man and horse at once.
sentences.n: stat is a present of memory: Nestor is old and telling this long after, and the centaur still “stands before my eyes”. sena is the distributive numeral for six, common in verse for sex. nodis is ablative of means, with conexis inter se “tied to one another” agreeing with it. hominem and equum are accusatives of respect with protectus — the Greek accusative, which verse uses freely with a participle of this kind.

sentences.t:
Codice qui misso, quem vix iuga bina moverent,
Tectaphon Oleniden a summo vertice fregit.
sentences.l: He, with a tree-trunk hurled that two yoked pairs could scarcely move, broke Tectaphos son of Olenus from the top of his crown.
sentences.i: He hurled a tree-trunk that two yoked teams could barely have shifted, and split Tectaphos, Olenus' son, from the crown of his head down.
sentences.n: Codice ... misso is an ablative absolute, “a trunk having been thrown”, and qui is a connecting relative, subject of fregit. quem ... moverent is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive, “such that they could scarcely move it”. iuga bina uses the distributive bina, regular with a noun that already means a pair. Oleniden is a Greek patronymic accusative.

sentences.t:
fracta volubilitas capitis latissima, perque os
perque cavas nares oculosque auresque cerebrum
molle fluit veluti concretum vimine querno
lac solet, utve liquor rari sub pondere cribri
manat et exprimitur per densa foramina spissus.
sentences.l: the head's very broad roundness was shattered, and through the mouth and through the hollow nostrils and the eyes and the ears the soft brain flows out, as curdled milk is accustomed to through oaken wickerwork, or as liquid trickles beneath the weight of a loose-woven sieve and is squeezed out thick through the close-set holes.
sentences.i: The wide round of his skull was smashed, and through mouth, hollow nostrils, eyes and ears the soft brain ran out, the way curdled milk drains through a basket of oak withies, or the way liquid seeps under the press of a wide-meshed sieve and is forced out thick through the packed holes.
sentences.n: volubilitas is “roundness, the quality of rolling”, used here of the shape of the skull, and est is understood with fracta. The four-fold perque ... perque ... -que ... -que is the epic way of listing by linked connectives. veluti ... solet introduces the first simile, with concretum lac “curdled milk” as subject of solet and fluere carried over from fluit; vimine querno is ablative, the cheese-maker's oak strainer. In the second simile rari “wide-meshed” and densa “close-set” describe the same sieve from two sides, and spissus “thick” is nominative with liquor but does the work of an adverb. Magnus prints a full stop at the end of the previous line and then a lower-case fracta here.

sentences.t:
Ast ego, dum parat hic armis nudare iacentem,
(scit tuus hoc genitor) gladium spoliantis in ima
ilia demisi.
sentences.l: But I, while he was preparing to strip the fallen man of his arms — your father knows this — sent my sword down into the lowest guts of the plunderer.
sentences.i: But I, while he was busy stripping the fallen man of his armour — your father knows it — drove my sword deep into the looter's belly.
sentences.n: Ast is the old poetic form of at “but”. armis nudare is “to strip bare of arms”, with the ablative of separation. The parenthesis appeals to a witness — the father of the man Nestor is addressing; Peleus has been fighting at 388–389. spoliantis is a present participle used as a noun in the genitive, “of the man plundering”, depending on ima ilia.

sentences.t:
Chthonius quoque Teleboasque
ense iacent nostro:
sentences.l: Chthonius too and Teleboas lie by our sword:
sentences.i: Chthonius too and Teleboas fell to my sword:
sentences.n: ense ... nostro is ablative of means with iacent, and nostro is again the plural standing for “my”. Here quoque is the adverb “also”. The present iacent gives the settled state: they lie dead.

sentences.t:
ramum prior ille bifurcum
gesserat, hic iaculum;
sentences.l: the former had carried a forked branch, this one a javelin;
sentences.i: The first had carried a forked branch, the second a javelin;
sentences.n: prior ille ... hic distributes the two names just given: ille the earlier of them, hic the nearer. gesserat is pluperfect — what each was carrying before the fight reached Nestor — and it has to be supplied again with hic iaculum.

sentences.t:
iaculo mihi vulnera fecit:
signa vides! adparet adhuc vetus inde cicatrix.
sentences.l: with the javelin he made wounds for me: you see the marks! an old scar from it still shows.
sentences.i: With that javelin he wounded me: you can see the marks! The old scar from it is still there.
sentences.n: mihi is dative of the person affected, “made wounds for me”, where English says “wounded me”; vulnera is a plural for a single wounding, ordinary in verse. inde is “from that source”, i.e. from the javelin. signa vides! is a plain present indicative used as a gesture, and adparet is present too — Nestor is showing the scar to his hearers as he speaks.

sentences.t:
Tunc ego debueram capienda ad Pergama mitti,
tum poteram magni, si non superare, morari
Hectoris arma meis!
sentences.l: Then I ought to have been sent to Pergama that had to be taken, then I could — if not overpower, at least delay — great Hector's arms with mine!
sentences.i: That was when I should have been sent to the taking of Troy; then I could have held off great Hector's weapons with my own, if not overpowered them!
sentences.n: debueram and poteram stand in the indicative where English wants “ought to have been” and “could have”: Latin puts the obligation or the possibility itself in the indicative and lets the unreality come from the context. capienda is a gerundive with ad, “to Pergama to be taken” = “to the taking of Pergama”. The phrase magni ... Hectoris arma is broken open by the parenthesis si non superare. meis is ablative, “with my own arms”.

sentences.t:
Illo sed tempore nullus,
aut puer Hector erat, nunc me mea deficit aetas.
sentences.l: But at that time Hector was nobody, or a boy; now my age fails me.
sentences.i: But in those days Hector was nothing, or a boy; and now my years fail me.
sentences.n: sed stands second in its clause, after Illo, which verse allows freely. nullus, “nobody, nothing”, is predicate with erat, and aut puer offers the milder alternative. In me mea deficit aetas the age is the subject and me the object: “my age abandons me”.

sentences.t:
Quid tibi victorem gemini Periphanta Pyraethi,
Ampyca quid referam, qui quadrupedantis Echecli
fixit in adverso cornum sine cuspide vultu?
sentences.l: Why should I tell you of Periphas, conqueror of twin-formed Pyraethus, why of Ampyx, who fixed a cornel-shaft without a point in the facing face of four-footed Echeclus?
sentences.i: Why tell you of Periphas, who beat two-formed Pyraethus, or of Ampyx, who planted a headless cornel shaft full in the face of four-footed Echeclus?
sentences.n: Quid ... referam is a deliberative subjunctive, “why should I relate?” — the figure by which a narrator lists what he claims to be passing over; the singular tibi keeps one hearer in view. victorem takes the genitive gemini Pyraethi. geminus “double” marks Pyraethus as two-natured, and quadrupedantis “going on four feet” does the same for Echeclus. cornum is the cornel-wood shaft named from its tree, and sine cuspide says it had no metal head.

sentences.t:
Vecte Pelethronium Macareus in pectus adacto
stravit Erigdupum, memini et venabula condi
inguine Nesseis manibus coniecta Cymeli.
sentences.l: Macareus laid Erigdupus low with a bar driven into his Pelethronian chest, and I remember hunting-spears, thrown by the hands of Nessus, being buried in the groin of Cymelus.
sentences.i: Macareus felled Erigdupus with a crowbar driven into his Pelethronian breast, and I remember hunting-spears from Nessus' hand buried in Cymelus' groin.
sentences.n: Vecte ... adacto is ablative of means, “with a bar driven home”, the participle agreeing with vecte. Pelethronium belongs with pectus: Pelethronium was a district of Thessaly the centaurs are at home in, so the adjective marks the victim as one of them. memini takes the accusative and infinitive venabula ... condi, “that hunting-spears were buried”. Nesseis is a possessive adjective from the name Nessus rather than a genitive of it.

sentences.t:
Nec tu credideris tantum cecinisse futura
Ampyciden Mopsum:
sentences.l: Nor should you believe that Ampyx's son Mopsus only sang of things to come:
sentences.i: And do not suppose that Mopsus, Ampyx's son, did nothing but prophesy the future:
sentences.n: nec with the perfect subjunctive credideris is the ordinary prohibition, “do not believe”. cecinisse is the perfect infinitive of cano, which is the verb of prophecy as much as of song; futura is the neuter plural future participle, “things about to be”. Ampyciden is a Greek patronymic accusative, “son of Ampyx”; an Ampyx fights at 450.

sentences.t:
Mopso iaculante biformis
accubuit frustraque loqui temptavit Hodites
ad mentum lingua mentoque ad guttura fixo.
sentences.l: With Mopsus hurling, the two-formed Hodites went down and tried in vain to speak, his tongue pinned to his chin and his chin to his throat.
sentences.i: When Mopsus threw, two-shaped Hodites went down and tried to speak and could not, his tongue nailed to his chin and his chin to his throat.
sentences.n: Mopso iaculante is an ablative absolute with a present participle, “Mopsus throwing”. biformis “two-shaped” is a standing epithet for a centaur. The closing ablative absolute is compressed: the single participle fixo agrees with mento and has to be understood again with lingua. accubuit is literally “lay down”, used of falling in death; some editions print occubuit, the more usual verb for meeting one's death.

sentences.t:
Quinque neci Caeneus dederat, Styphelumque Bromumque
Antimachumque Elymumque securiferumque Pyraechmen:
sentences.l: Caeneus had given five to death, Styphelus and Bromus and Antimachus and Elymus and axe-bearing Pyraechmes:
sentences.i: Caeneus had killed five: Styphelus, Bromus, Antimachus, Elymus, and Pyraechmes with his axe:
sentences.n: neci dederat is the dative idiom “had given over to death”, the same construction as the leto dederat that opened this part. The five names are strung together on repeated -que, the epic polysyndeton, and securiferum “axe-bearing” is a compound adjective of the sort epic likes. Magnus prints Pyraechmen, a Greek accusative in -en; some editions print the different name-form Pyracmon.

sentences.t: vulnera non memini, numerum nomenque notavi.
sentences.l: I do not remember the wounds; the number and the name I noted.
sentences.i: I don't remember how they were wounded; I marked the count and the names.
sentences.n: The two halves stand side by side without a connective, and the alliteration numerum nomenque notavi carries the point: Nestor's memory kept the tally and not the detail. nomen is singular for the five names taken together.

sentences.t:
Provolat Emathii spoliis armatus Alesi,
quem dederat leto, membris et corpore Latreus
maximus:
sentences.l: Forward flies Latreus, armed with the spoils of Emathian Alesus, whom he had given to death, greatest in limbs and body:
sentences.i: Out charged Latreus, wearing the armour stripped from Emathian Alesus, whom he had killed — huge in limb and body:
sentences.n: Provolat is a historic present, and the verb stands first for the rush of it. armatus takes the ablative spoliis, “armed with the spoils”; Emathius is Macedonian or Thessalian. The relative clause quem dederat leto uses the same “give over to death” idiom as the neci dederat said of Caeneus at 459, with leto for neci. membris et corpore are ablatives of respect with maximus.

sentences.t:
huic aetas inter iuvenemque senemque,
vis iuvenalis erat, variabant tempora cani.
sentences.l: for him the age was between a young man and an old man, his strength was youthful, grey hairs dappled his temples.
sentences.i: His age lay between young and old; his strength was a young man's; grey hairs streaked his temples.
sentences.n: huic is dative of possession, “to him there was an age” = “his age was”, and the one erat serves both aetas and vis. inter iuvenemque senemque uses the two persons for the two stages of life. variabant is “made varied, dappled”, and its subject is cani, “the grey ones”, i.e. grey hairs.

sentences.t:
Qui clipeo gladioque Macedoniaque sarisa
conspicuus faciemque obversus in agmen utrumque
armaque concussit certumque equitavit in orbem
verbaque tot fudit vacuas animosus in auras:
sentences.l: He, conspicuous with shield and sword and Macedonian pike, and turned in face towards both battle-lines, both shook his arms and rode round in a fixed circle and poured out so many words, high-spirited, into the empty air:
sentences.i: Conspicuous with shield, sword and Macedonian pike, turning his face on both armies, he shook his weapons, wheeled his horse in a set circle, and flung all these words into the empty air:
sentences.n: Qui is a connecting relative, “and he”. faciem is a Greek accusative of respect with obversus, “turned as to his face”, the participle passive in form and middle in sense. The three verbs are strung with -que ... -que ... -que. certum in orbem is “in a measured circle”. A sarisa is the long Macedonian pike, an anachronism Ovid does not disguise. animosus, nominative, does the work of an adverb. Magnus prints gladioque “and sword”; some editions print galeaque, “and helmet”.

sentences.t:
“Et te, Caeni, feram? Nam tu mihi femina semper,
tu mihi Caenis eris.
sentences.l: “And shall I endure you as well, Caenis? For to me you will always be a woman, to me you will be Caenis.
sentences.i: “Am I to put up with you too, Caenis? To me you will always be a woman; to me you will be Caenis.
sentences.n: Caeni is the vocative of the woman's name Caenis, not of Caeneus — Latreus refuses the man's name in his first word, and the whole taunt runs on that refusal. mihi is dative of the person judging, “to me, in my view”. The single eris serves both halves, with semper in the first.

sentences.t:
Nec te natalis origo
commonuit, mentemque subit, quo praemia facto
quaque viri falsam speciem mercede parasti?
sentences.l: Did your birth-origin not remind you, and does it not enter your mind by what deed you got your rewards and at what wage the false appearance of a man?
sentences.i: Did your birth not remind you? Does it not come into your mind by what act you won your prize, and at what price you got the false shape of a man?
sentences.n: The one nec governs both verbs, the perfect commonuit and the present subit. quo ... facto and qua ... mercede are ablatives in the question that depends on subit, and parasti governs two objects, praemia “the rewards” and viri falsam speciem “the false appearance of a man”. Magnus prints parasti, the syncopated perfect indicative for paravisti; some editions print pararis, the perfect subjunctive an indirect question normally takes. viri falsam speciem is Latreus's own phrase and his contempt: he grants the shape and denies the thing.

sentences.t:
Quid sis nata, vide, vel quid sis passa, columque,
i, cape cum calathis et stamina pollice torque:
bella relinque viris.”
sentences.l: See what you were born, or what you suffered, and go, take the distaff along with the wool-baskets, and twist the threads with your thumb: leave wars to men.”
sentences.i: Look what you were born as, or what you suffered; go on, take up the distaff and the wool-baskets and twist your thread with your thumb — leave war to men.”
sentences.n: Quid sis nata and quid sis passa are indirect questions with the subjunctive after vide. passa is the perfect participle of the deponent patior and is active in sense, “having suffered” — “what you suffered”, not “what was suffered”. Both nata and passa are feminine, so the grammar itself carries the taunt: Latreus will not let the participles agree with a man. The distaff, the wool-baskets and the spun thread are the standing Roman signs of a woman's work, so the order means “go back to being a woman”. viris, dative, picks up the viri of 473. i is the imperative of eo, one letter long.

sentences.t:
Iactanti talia Caeneus
extentum cursu missa latus eruit hasta,
qua vir equo commissus erat.
sentences.l: On him flinging out such things Caeneus tore open the flank stretched out by his running, with a spear thrown, where the man had been joined to the horse.
sentences.i: As he flung out this boasting, Caeneus threw his spear and ripped open the flank stretched long by his galloping, at the point where the man was joined to the horse.
sentences.n: Iactanti is a dative participle used as a noun, “to the one boasting such things”, and with eruit latus it works as a dative of disadvantage: he tore open the boaster's flank. missa ... hasta is ablative of means. extentum cursu is “stretched out by his running”, the body pulled long at the gallop. qua is the relative adverb “at the point where”, and commissus erat is pluperfect passive of committo, “had been joined”.

sentences.t:
Furit ille dolore
nudaque Phyllei iuvenis ferit ora sarisa.
sentences.l: He rages with the pain and strikes the bare face of the Phyllean youth with his pike.
sentences.i: He went mad with the pain and struck the bare face of the young man from Phyllus with his pike.
sentences.n: dolore is ablative of cause with furit. Phyllei iuvenis is Caeneus, named from Phyllus in Thessaly, and the genitive depends on ora. nuda ... ora is the unarmoured face: Latreus aims where a helmet would be. sarisa is ablative of means, the Macedonian pike again.

sentences.t:
Non secus haec resilit, quam tecti a culmine grando,
aut siquis parvo feriat cava tympana saxo.
sentences.l: It springs back not otherwise than hail from a roof's ridge, or if someone should strike hollow drums with a small stone.
sentences.i: It bounced off exactly as hail does from a roof-ridge, or as a pebble would if someone struck a hollow drum with it.
sentences.n: Non secus ... quam is the correlative “not otherwise than”, that is “just as”. haec is the sarisa, feminine, as subject of resilit. The second limb changes construction: siquis ... feriat is a potential subjunctive, “if anyone should strike”, so the comparison is with what would happen rather than with what does. cava tympana are hand-drums; what is compared is the rebound and the noise.

sentences.t:
Comminus adgreditur laterique recondere duro
luctatur gladium: gladio loca pervia non sunt.
sentences.l: Hand to hand he attacks and struggles to bury his sword in the hard flank: for the sword the places are not passable.
sentences.i: He closed and fought to sink his sword into the hard flank: there was no way through for the sword.
sentences.n: adgreditur is deponent and active in sense. luctatur takes the infinitive recondere, “struggles to hide away”, recondo being the ordinary verb for burying a blade in a body. lateri ... duro is dative with the compound verb. gladio is dative of reference, “passable for a sword”, and the repetition gladium: gladio straight across the colon is the point.

sentences.t:
“Haud tamen effugies! medio iugulaberis ense,
quandoquidem mucro est hebes” inquit et in latus ensem
obliquat longaque amplectitur ilia dextra.
sentences.l: “Still, you will not escape! You will have your throat cut with the middle of the blade, since the point is blunt,” he says, and slants his sword into the flank and with his long right hand takes his loins in a grip all round.
sentences.i: “You won't get away even so! The point is blunt, so you'll have your throat cut with the middle of the blade,” he said, and turned the sword sideways into the flank and reached his right arm right round his loins.
sentences.n: iugulaberis is future passive of iugulo, “to cut the throat”; medio ... ense is ablative of means, “with the middle of the blade”, that is with its edge, because the mucro, the point, will not go in. quandoquidem “since indeed” gives the reason. longa agrees with dextra, the right hand stretched out far, so that amplectitur ilia describes the sweep of the arm round the horse-body rather than an embrace.

sentences.t:
Plaga facit gemitus in corpore marmoris icti,
fractaque dissiluit percusso lammina callo.
sentences.l: The blow makes groans as in a body of struck marble, and the blade, broken, sprang apart, the hard skin having been struck.
sentences.i: The stroke rang as it rings in a block of struck marble, and the blade shattered and flew off the hardened hide.
sentences.n: Plaga is the stroke and gemitus, accusative plural, the sounds it makes. marmoris icti is genitive with corpore, “in the mass of struck marble”, and the comparison is left compressed, with no word for “as if”. lammina is the double-l spelling of lamina, the blade-plate. percusso ... callo is an ablative absolute, callum being the hardened skin on which the blade breaks. Magnus prints in corpore marmoris icti; some editions print ut corpore marmoris icto, which supplies the missing word of comparison.

sentences.t:
Ut satis inlaesos miranti praebuit artus,
“nunc age,” ait Caeneus, “nostro tua corpora ferro
temptemus!”
sentences.l: When he had offered his unharmed limbs long enough to the man marvelling at them, “now come,” says Caeneus, “let us try your body with our iron!”
sentences.i: When he had let the man wonder at his unhurt limbs long enough, “now then,” said Caeneus, “let's test your body with my steel!”
sentences.n: Ut with the perfect praebuit is temporal, “when”; satis goes with praebuit, “offered enough”. miranti is a dative participle used as a noun, “to the one wondering”. temptemus is a hortatory subjunctive. nostro ... tua ... ferro repeats the pattern of Nestor's own taunt to Dorylas at 384, and corpora is the poetic plural for a single body.

sentences.t:
capuloque tenus demisit in armos
ensem fatiferum caecumque in viscera movit
versavitque manu vulnusque in vulnere fecit.
sentences.l: and right up to the hilt he sent his death-bringing sword down into the shoulders and moved it, unseeing, into the guts and turned it with his hand and made a wound within the wound.
sentences.i: and he drove his death-dealing sword in up to the hilt, into the shoulders, worked it blind into the guts, twisted it with his hand and made a wound inside the wound.
sentences.n: capulo tenus is the postposition tenus with the ablative, “as far as the hilt”. caecum agrees with ensem: the blade is “blind”, which can mean either seeing nothing or unseen, and both work here — it goes in out of sight inside the body. The four verbs are chained together on repeated -que, and vulnus in vulnere fecit is the figure of one noun twice over in two cases. Magnus prints manu, ablative, “with his hand”; some editions print manum, which would make the hand the object of versavit.

sentences.t:
Ecce ruunt vasto rabidi clamore bimembres
telaque in hunc omnes unum mittuntque feruntque.
sentences.l: Look — the two-limbed ones rush in raging with a huge shout, and all of them both hurl and drive their weapons against this one man.
sentences.i: Then the two-bodied creatures charged in raving, with a huge roar, and every one of them threw or drove his weapon at this single man.
sentences.n: bimembres, “two-limbed”, is a third word for the centaurs in this part, beside semiferos and biformis. vasto ... clamore is ablative of attendant circumstance. mittunt and ferunt distinguish the weapon thrown from the one kept in the hand and driven home. omnes against in hunc ... unum is the whole point of the line: all of them against one.

sentences.t:
Tela retusa cadunt: manet inperfossus ab omni
inque cruentatus Caeneus Elateius ictu.
sentences.l: The weapons fall blunted: Caeneus son of Elatus stays unpierced and unbloodied by every blow.
sentences.i: Their weapons fell blunted: Caeneus, Elatus' son, stayed unpierced and unbloodied by every stroke.
sentences.n: inque cruentatus is a tmesis: the compound incruentatus “unbloodied” is split open and the -que planted inside it, so the reader has to put the word back together. inperfossus, “not pierced through”, is the negative compound beside it, in the edition's inp- spelling. ab omni ... ictu is ab with the ablative of a thing, “by every blow”, doing duty for an agent. Elateius is a patronymic adjective, “son of Elatus”.

sentences.t: Fecerat attonitos nova res.
sentences.l: The strange thing had made them thunderstruck.
sentences.i: The novelty left them stunned.
sentences.n: nova res is “the new thing, the unheard-of event”, and attonitos, literally “thunderstruck”, is a predicate accusative with fecerat. The pluperfect steps back a moment behind the surrounding narrative.

sentences.t:
“Heu dedecus ingens!”
Monychus exclamat, “populus superamur ab uno
vixque viro:
sentences.l: “Alas, a huge disgrace!” Monychus cries out, “we, a whole people, are beaten by one, and hardly a man:
sentences.i: “What a huge disgrace!” Monychus shouted. “A whole people, and we are beaten by one — and hardly a man at that:
sentences.n: dedecus ingens is an accusative of exclamation after heu. populus is nominative, standing in apposition to the “we” already inside superamur; the verb carries its own subject and the noun simply leans on it. ab uno is the agent with the passive. vix ... viro keeps Latreus's jeer alive: scarcely a man.

sentences.t:
quamquam ille vir est, nos segnibus actis
quod fuit ille, sumus!
sentences.l: although he is a man, we, by our sluggish doings, are what he was!
sentences.i: though he is a man — and we, with our slack performance, are what he used to be!
sentences.n: quamquam takes the indicative est, a real concession: Monychus grants the manhood he has just denied. segnibus actis is ablative of cause, “by our sluggish deeds”. quod fuit ille is a relative clause standing as the predicate of sumus, “we are the thing he was” — and what he was is the female name Latreus threw at him, said here without being said.

sentences.t: Quid membra inmania prosunt?
sentences.l: What good are our monstrous limbs?
sentences.n: prosum takes a dative of the person helped, here left unexpressed, and Quid is the adverbial accusative, “to what good?”. inmania is the edition's spelling for immania.

sentences.t:
Quid geminae vires et quod fortissima rerum
in nobis duplex natura animalia iunxit?
sentences.l: What good our doubled strength, and that a twofold nature has joined in us the strongest creatures of all?
sentences.i: What good is our doubled strength, and the fact that a two-fold nature has joined in us the strongest animals there are?
sentences.n: quod ... iunxit is a noun clause, “the fact that it joined”, standing as a second subject of the prosunt carried over from the question before. fortissima rerum animalia is “the strongest creatures of all”, rerum being a partitive genitive that verse uses freely after a superlative.

sentences.t:
Nec nos matre dea, nec nos Ixione natos
esse reor, qui tantus erat, Iunonis ut altae
spem caperet:
sentences.l: Nor do I think that we were born of a goddess mother, nor of Ixion, who was so great that he conceived a hope of lofty Juno:
sentences.i: I don't believe we were born of a goddess for a mother, or of Ixion, who was great enough to form a hope of Juno on high:
sentences.n: reor takes the accusative and infinitive nos ... natos esse, with the negative nec doubled for the two parents. matre dea and Ixione are ablatives of origin with natos. qui tantus erat ... ut ... caperet is a result clause. Ixion is the centaurs' father in the standing story, and the hope he conceived of Juno is what he was punished for; Monychus is arguing that the descent cannot be true of creatures who fight like this.

sentences.t: nos semimari superamur ab hoste!
sentences.l: we are beaten by a half-male enemy!
sentences.i: we are being beaten by a half-man for an enemy!
sentences.n: semimari is the ablative of semimas, “half-male”, agreeing with hoste; it is Monychus's third word for Caeneus, after uno and vix viro, and it is meant to wound. nos stands first for the contrast with the enemy.

sentences.t:
Saxa trabesque super totosque involvite montes
vivacemque animam missis elidite silvis!
sentences.l: Roll rocks and beams and whole mountains on top of him, and crush out his tenacious life with forests hurled down!
sentences.i: Pile rocks and beams and whole mountains on him, and squeeze out that stubborn life under hurled forests!
sentences.n: involvite and elidite are imperatives. super is best taken as the adverb “on top”, since saxa, trabes and montes are all accusative objects of involvite. vivacem animam is “the long-lived breath”, vivax being what will not stop living. missis ... silvis is ablative of means, whole woods standing for the timber.

sentences.t: silva premat fauces, et erit pro vulnere pondus.”
sentences.l: let a forest press his throat, and the weight will be in place of a wound.”
sentences.i: let the timber crush his windpipe, and the weight will serve instead of a wound.”
sentences.n: premat is a jussive subjunctive, “let it press”. fauces is the throat taken as the passage for breath. pro vulnere is “in place of a wound”: since nothing will pierce him, weight has to do the work. Magnus prints silva “a wood”; some editions print massa, “a mass”.

sentences.t:
Dixit et insanis deiectam viribus austri
forte trabem nactus validum coniecit in hostem
exemplumque fuit, parvoque in tempore nudus
arboris Othrys erat, nec habebat Pelion umbras.
sentences.l: He spoke, and having by chance got hold of a beam brought down by the mad strength of the south wind, he hurled it at his powerful enemy and was a precedent, and in a short time Othrys was bare of tree, nor did Pelion have shade.
sentences.i: He spoke, and chancing on a beam that the south wind's mad force had brought down, he hurled it at his strong enemy and set the example; and in a little while Othrys was stripped of its trees, and Pelion had no shade left.
sentences.n: nactus is the perfect participle of the deponent nanciscor and is active in sense, “having got hold of”. forte is the ablative of fors, “by chance”, not a form of fortis. deiectam ... viribus austri is “brought down by the strength of the south wind”, with insanis “raving” personifying the gale. exemplum fuit, “he was a precedent”, means the rest of them copied him. nudus takes the genitive arboris, “bare of tree”, the singular for the whole growth; Othrys and Pelion are the two Thessalian mountains this fighting is set among.

sentences.t:
Obrutus inmani tumulo sub pondere Caeneus
aestuat arboreo congestaque robora duris
fert umeris.
sentences.l: Buried by a monstrous mound, Caeneus seethes beneath the weight of the trees and carries the heaped-up oaks on his hard shoulders.
sentences.i: Buried under a monstrous mound, Caeneus struggled beneath the weight of timber, carrying the piled oak on his hard shoulders.
sentences.n: Obrutus is passive, “overwhelmed”, with inmani tumulo as ablative of means; tumulus is also the word for a burial mound. sub pondere in 514 is left waiting for its adjective arboreo, which does not arrive until the second word of 515, after aestuat. aestuat is “boils, heaves”, the verb for a sea or a fever, here of a man labouring under a load. robora are oaks, the hardest of the timber. Magnus prints tumulo; some editions print cumulo, “heap”.

sentences.t:
Sed enim postquam super ora caputque
crevit onus neque habet, quas ducat, spiritus auras,
sentences.l: But indeed, after the load grew above his face and head and his breath has not the airs which it might draw,
sentences.i: But once the load had risen above his face and head, and his breath had no air left to draw,
sentences.n: Sed enim is the epic “but in fact”, marking the turn. postquam takes the perfect crevit and then the present habet: Latin allows the tenses to shift inside a single temporal clause. quas ducat is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive, “airs for him to draw”, and it sits between habet and its own antecedent auras. ducere auras is the ordinary phrase for drawing breath.

sentences.t:
deficit interdum, modo se super aera frustra
tollere conatur iactasque evolvere silvas,
interdumque movet, veluti, quam cernimus, ecce,
ardua si terrae quatiatur motibus Ide.
sentences.l: at times he fails, at times he tries in vain to lift himself up into the air above and to roll off the woods thrown on him, and at times he moves them — just as, if steep Ida, the one we can see, look, were shaken by movements of the earth.
sentences.i: sometimes he gave out, sometimes he tried and failed to heave himself up into the air and roll the piled woods off, and sometimes he did shift them — just as if steep Ida, the one we can see from here, look, were shaken by an earthquake.
sentences.n: interdum ... modo ... interdumque is the “now ... now” series, three times over. aera is the Greek accusative of aer. quam cernimus, ecce is Nestor breaking off to point: Ida is in sight from where he is speaking, so the simile is a gesture as much as a comparison. si ... quatiatur is present subjunctive in an imagined comparison, “as if it were being shaken”, and terrae motibus is the plain phrase for an earthquake.

sentences.t:
Exitus in dubio est: alii sub inania corpus
Tartara detrusum silvarum mole ferebant;
sentences.l: The outcome is in doubt: some used to report that the body had been thrust down into empty Tartarus by the mass of the woods;
sentences.i: How it ended is uncertain: some maintained that the mass of timber had shoved his body down to the void of Tartarus;
sentences.n: Exitus in dubio est answers the Auctor in incerto est of 419: Nestor twice admits that he does not know. ferebant is “they used to report”, with an accusative and infinitive whose esse is left out — corpus ... detrusum (esse). inania Tartara is neuter plural, the usual form of the name. silvarum mole is ablative of means.

sentences.t:
abnuit Ampycides medioque ex aggere fulvis
vidit avem pennis liquidas exire sub auras,
quae mihi tum primum, tunc est conspecta supremum.
sentences.l: The son of Ampyx denied it, and saw a bird with tawny wings go out from the middle of the mound into the clear air, a bird which was then seen by me for the first time and then for the last.
sentences.i: The son of Ampyx said no, and saw a bird with tawny wings come out of the middle of the pile into the open air — a bird I saw then for the first time and then for the last.
sentences.n: abnuit is “shook the head”, the gesture standing for the denial. Ampycides is the patronymic by which Mopsus is named. fulvis pennis is ablative of description, “with tawny feathers”; fulvis ends 524 and pennis comes only in 525, with vidit avem standing between them. tum and tunc, both “then”, are set against primum “for the first time” and supremum “for the last”, supremum being an adverbial accusative. mihi is dative of the agent with the passive conspecta est, ordinary with a perfect passive.

sentences.t:
Hanc ubi lustrantem leni sua castra volatu
Mopsus et ingenti circum clangore sonantem
adspexit pariterque animis oculisque secutus
“o salve” dixit,
sentences.l: When Mopsus caught sight of her circling his own camp with gentle flight and sounding round about with a huge clangour, and followed her alike with his mind and his eyes, he said “oh, hail,”
sentences.i: When Mopsus saw her wheeling over his own camp on an easy wing and ringing out around it with a huge cry, and followed her with his mind as much as his eyes, he said: “Hail,”
sentences.n: Hanc, “her”, is the bird of the sentence before, and both participles agree with it, lustrantem in 527 and sonantem at the end of 528, with the whole of Mopsus's name and the noise-phrase standing between them. ubi with the perfect adspexit is temporal, “when”. leni ... volatu and ingenti ... clangore are ablatives of manner. animis oculisque, “with mind and eyes alike”, is a standing pairing.

sentences.t:
“Lapithaeae gloria gentis,
maxime vir quondam, sed nunc avis unica, Caeneu!”
sentences.l: “glory of the Lapith race, once greatest of men, but now a bird without a fellow, Caeneus!”
sentences.i: “glory of the Lapith people, once the greatest of men, but now a bird without a fellow — Caeneus!”
sentences.n: Every word of the address is vocative: gloria, maxime vir, avis unica, and, held back to the very end, the name — Caeneu, the Greek vocative of Caeneus, the man's name and not the woman's that Latreus used. unica is “one of a kind”, there being no second such bird. quondam against nunc gives the whole shape of the greeting.

sentences.t: Credita res auctore suo est:
sentences.l: The thing was believed on account of its own guarantor:
sentences.i: We believed it because of who said it:
sentences.n: Credita est is perfect passive of credo with res as subject; auctore suo is ablative of cause, “on account of its own authority” — Mopsus's word was enough. auctor answers the auctor of 419, the unknown thrower of the javelin: the word covers the doer of a deed and the guarantor of a story alike.

sentences.t:
dolor addidit iram,
oppressumque aegre tulimus tot ab hostibus unum;
sentences.l: grief added anger, and we bore it hard that one man had been crushed by so many enemies;
sentences.i: grief brought anger with it, and we took it hard that one man had been overwhelmed by so many enemies;
sentences.n: aegre tulimus is the idiom “we bore it ill”, that is, we resented it, and it takes an accusative and infinitive with esse understood: oppressum ... unum (esse). tot ab hostibus is the agent with the passive participle. unum against tot repeats the one-against-many that Monychus complained of.

sentences.t:
nec prius abstitimus ferro exercere dolorem,
quam data pars leto, partem fuga noxque removit.”
sentences.l: nor did we leave off plying our grief with the sword before a part had been given to death, and flight and night had taken a part away.”
sentences.i: and we did not stop working our grief out with the sword until one part of them had been killed and flight and darkness had carried off the rest.”
sentences.n: prius ... quam is split apart, “not sooner ... than”, that is “not until”. abstitimus takes the infinitive exercere, “we stood off from plying”, and ferro is ablative of means. data (est) pars leto uses the same leto dare idiom that opened this part. The two halves balance, pars ... partem, one killed and the other carried off, with removit singular for the two subjects fuga and nox. Nestor's speech ends here.
